text: MOLECULAR DYNAMICS / THERMOSTATS Thermostats: temperature control and distributions Compare fluctuations, ergodicity and time correlations as well as mean temperature, from Nosé–Hoover and velocity rescaling to stochastic and momentum-conserving methods. Retain the earlier two-method comparison of Langevin and CSVR. Preserve the earlier one-degree-of-freedom harmonic Langevin/BAOAB case. A separate edition compares both baths with the same OBABO splitting for a nondegenerate two-degree harmonic system and a two-degree anharmonic system with quartic coefficient lambda=0.2, and checks the standalone CSVR kinetic-energy kernel. A separate fixed two-mode release contrasts direct rescaling, Berendsen, Nosé–Hoover and NHC3 while retaining unmet or unresolved original goals. The remaining six methods are planned. JSON · Markdown Define the controlled temperature With kinetic energy K and f active degrees of freedom, the kinetic temperature is T = 2 K / (f k_B). Count constraints and removed center-of-mass motion consistently, and separate thermal motion from streaming. State whether rotational degrees of freedom are included. Equal mean temperature does not imply equal distributions For f independent momentum degrees of freedom with classical quadratic kinetic energy, canonical equilibrium gives 2 K/(k_B T₀) a chi-square distribution with f degrees of freedom. Its mean K is f k_B T₀/2 and variance is f(k_B T₀)²/2. Direct rescaling v ← √(T₀/T) v fixes K immediately after application, removing these fluctuations. CSVR instead uses a stochastic factor to generate fluctuations. Separate sampling from dynamics An invariant distribution does not ensure adequate finite-time exploration. Even correct equilibrium sampling can coexist with friction- or collision-induced changes in velocity autocorrelations and diffusion. Assess integration error, heat-bath coupling time and random-seed dependence. CSVR and Langevin: shared canonical targets, distinct correlations The new comparison is limited to small classical systems. CSVR and Langevin use matched OBABO splitting, degrees of freedom, temperature, potential and observation times. Distribution, fluctuations and correlations are separate diagnostics. The earlier BAOAB harmonic results remain in their original release. The stochastic CSVR update and its sign CSVR evolves the total kinetic energy stochastically and scales all momenta together. The implementation uses the 2007 kinetic-energy SDE and exact propagator, with the signed factor in the 2008 paper. Here h denotes a thermostat substep. The same Gaussian R determines energy and sign. Momentum flips matter for a few degrees of freedom. Check momentum, kinetic energy and instantaneous-temperature distributions, means and variances. Position references are analytic for harmonic systems and use separate quadrature for the anharmonic case. Matching the mean temperature alone does not check fluctuations. Dynamic correlations depend on the method and coupling time. Measure position q, momentum p, kinetic energy K and total energy H without requiring agreement between methods. For harmonic Langevin, distinguish the continuous matrix exponential from the OBABO discrete stationary covariance/propagator. Other full-system correlations are measured with uncertainty and timestep dependence. The exact ρK(t)=exp(−t/τ) reference applies only to the isolated bath. Full harmonic or anharmonic motion exchanges K and U, so that expression is not used as its correlation target. CDF errors are maxima over predeclared checkpoints: five position/energy points and, for the conditional bath, three quantile points. They are not Kolmogorov–Smirnov suprema over the whole distribution. Full-system correlations use canonical-reference centering and normalization, so finite-step zero-lag values need not equal one exactly. Use independent replicas, fixed seeds and finite observation windows; separate sampling uncertainty from timestep and coupling effects. These small tests do not guarantee mixing from arbitrary starts. Correlation standard errors use the spread of products across independent replicas at each lag; they are not uncertainties of a single-trajectory time average or an effective-sample-size estimate. No independent dynamical reference is claimed for the anharmonic full-system correlations, which are not presented as having zero error. A common scaling factor does not directly randomize momentum direction. A correct K distribution cannot rule out restricted sampling from invariant conditions such as zero total momentum in a symmetric system, or from invariant subspaces. The adopted degrees of freedom include no added constraints or removed center-of-mass mode. For a positive bath step, at K=0 the direction is undefined, so this implementation rejects global rescaling explicitly. It does not inject an arbitrary direction as an undocumented algorithm. Nonfinite or nonphysical parameters are also checked. Sources: Canonical sampling through velocity rescaling Primary sources for the adopted equations G. Bussi, D. Donadio and M. Parrinello (2007). Exact CSVR bath: conditional laws, fluctuations and kinetic correlation · ZIP · Stored results · Rerun receipt A bath diagnostic, not another independent physical problem. Eight foundational entries Direct velocity rescaling Multiply velocities by a common factor to set the kinetic energy at each application. Simple deterministic rescaling does not reproduce canonical kinetic-energy fluctuations. A comparison case for distinguishing temperature control from canonical sampling. Ratio-based rescaling is undefined at T=0; the application interval also matters. Each entry exposes fixed inputs, measurements, errors/uncertainty, criteria, code, tests, ZIP and independent-extraction receipt. The earlier BAOAB example is separate evidence. These CSVR comparisons are not evidence for other algorithms. A separate fixed-input release contrasts four deterministic schemes and retains unmet/unresolved original goals; six other schemes remain planned. Sources and review scope For CSVR, the kinetic-energy equations/appendix in the 2007 author manuscript, signed update in the 2008 manuscript and author correction were checked. The adopted small classical examples are validated by separate references, quadrature and actual reruns. They do not reproduce the original Lennard–Jones or TIP4P-water experiments. This CSVR source audit is not transferred to other algorithms. Four deterministic schemes have a separate limited release; the remaining six schemes are comparative reading and primary-source entry points. Individual original-paper curation for Gaussian isokinetic remains open. Citation and reuse · Method registry / JSON
